raw_plan.promise: The praise a cohort already gives you can become publishable testimonials, because the ask becomes one structured request with a bounded follow-up schedule you set once instead of a decision you re-make per student.
raw_plan.orientation: Senja is where you ask your cohort for a testimonial — students get a short page where they leave a few sentences or a video — and where the answers sit afterwards so you can put them on your course page.
raw_plan.arc: One email, one move. Open on the part of the job this reader actually postpones (the ask, and the second ask), show the mechanism that makes the chasing a setting rather than a weekly decision, hand them the student-side cost so the ask stops feeling heavy, and close on a free signup with one invite as the test. Because it stands alone, nothing may be deferred: the mechanism, its bounded limits and the next step all appear in this email.
raw_plan.sequence_rationale: One email was requested in so many words, so the whole argument has to fit a single read. I chose the invite-and-follow-up mechanism over three rival angles. (a) The course-platform trigger (E49/E48) is the most seductive angle and the wrong lead: it needs a paid plan and a connected platform, and the only evidence of platform use is one creator's 2022 retrospective — the research explicitly warns against making a partner integration the primary proposition for a segment that was not selected on that basis. (b) Display and reuse (E99, E24, E103, E159) argues about the destination to a reader who has nothing to display yet. (c) Price (the strongest shelf by count) wins arguments for a reader who is comparing vendors; this one is not — they are stuck before the collection step. The invite mechanism is the only angle that is LEAD-ranked, linked by the current dossier to two verified problems (P1, P3), and usable on a free account with no prerequisite. Objection selection: P1's reluctance ("I don't want to seem pushy") is grounded and applies directly to the requested step, and there is product evidence for a real answer — follow-ups are optional and bounded to three, only non-responders get them, and the student side is about thirty seconds with no account. What remains unanswerable, and is therefore kept out of the copy rather than handed to the writer: nothing in the material establishes how students actually react to the reminders, what response rate to expect, or that well-timed asks produce stronger testimonials. emails.single_idea: You are not short of goodwill from your cohort — you are short of a second ask, and that one can be a setting instead of a decision you make per student.
emails.felt_need: "People say lovely things in the Slack channel and at the end of a chapter, and almost none of it ends up as something I can put on the cohort page. I know I'm supposed to ask. I don't know how to ask without feeling like I'm chasing my own students, so I ask once, late, and let it go."
emails.status_quo: The ask is handmade. A rating-and-comment box at the end of a module, praise that arrives in a community channel or a DM, and a mental note to follow up with the two people who said something quotable — documented in creators' own accounts of collecting feedback for their course and cohort offers.
emails.why_it_fails: A handmade ask only reaches whoever happens to be in the room, and the follow-up is a separate act of will per person: one message, written by you, to someone you have to remember to write to. So the first ask goes out and the second one never does, and the student whose answer you wanted most is the one you forget.
emails.mechanism: One form, one list. You invite the cohort from Senja individually or in bulk, and you turn on up to three follow-up emails that go out 1, 3 and 7 days after the invite — only to students who have not responded yet. The chasing stops being something you decide each week and becomes something you decided once. On the student's side it is a personalised page where they leave text or a video in about thirty seconds, with no account to create and nothing to install, so the thing you are asking for is genuinely small. One condition to state plainly: follow-ups only apply to invites sent after you turn them on, so switch them on before you send.

alternative_arguments.selection_reason: A different commercial bet for the same slot: not reach and persistence, but control and permission. P2 is grounded — this reader is openly unsure whether to ask for video or writing and where any of it can legitimately go. alternative_arguments.argument_issue: These are capability facts about form setup. They cannot establish which format produces better testimonials, nor that students are comfortable on camera. The claim must stay on who decides what — you decide the format, they decide the permission.
alternative_arguments.single_idea: You choose the format of the answer; your student chooses whether you can publish it — and both of those are settings on the form, not a negotiation you have over email.
alternative_arguments.felt_need: "Do I ask for video or just written? If I ask for video, am I making it awkward? And once someone sends me something nice, am I actually allowed to put it on my sales page?"
alternative_arguments.status_quo: The permission conversation happens by hand, after the fact: a nice message arrives, and you write back to ask whether you can quote it and whether you can use their name.
alternative_arguments.why_it_fails: Asking for permission after the answer turns one request into two, and the second one arrives when the student has already moved on — so the quotable line sits in your inbox unused because nobody ever said yes out loud.
